newsitem.title: JAPAN: Beatles auction kicks off at high price.
newsitem.headline: Beatles auction kicks off at high price.

text.p: The original birth certificate of Sir Paul McCartney sold for 10.35 million yen ($84,146) on Saturday in the biggest-ever auction of Beatles memorabilia.

The certificate, the first of 300 items to go on the block in a sale expected to last for four hours, brought a far higher price than the pre-sale estimate of $13,000. The sale price includes the 15 percent commission for the auction house.
The buyer was an unidentified party in London while the seller was a record collector from California, auction house officials said.
McCartney has recently denounced the soaring trade in pop music memorabilia, singling out his lack of ownership of his own birth certificate.

"To show how ridiculous this whole memorabilia market has become, there is currently someone in the United States who owns my own birth certificate," he said. "How people can feel that that is right is beyond my comprehension."
The certificate, which records McCartney's June 18, 1942, birth in Liverpool, England, had first been sold by McCartney's stepmother after the death of his father.
McCartney was successful in stopping part of the sale.
On Friday he obtained an injunction against Bonhams to halt the planned sale of the original lyrics to "Penny Lane," one of the Beatles' biggest hits.
Geoff Baker, spokesman for the recently knighted Beatle, said he believed the owner of the Number One hit was not entitled to sell the draft, which had been valued at $79,780.
Bonham officials expect the auction, which also includes the only guitar signed by all four musicians, to set world record prices for pop music souvenirs.
Three decades after Beatlemania swept Japan and the rest of the world, Tokyo was chosen as the site of Saturday's auction because the "Fab Four" music is again topping charts in Japan.

Other items on sale are the Liverpool house where Ringo Starr was born, the Steinway piano John Lennon used to compose his classic song "Imagine" and a road stud from London's Abbey Road crossing which inspired the album and has a reserve price of about $500.
"The response we have had to the auction is phenomenal," said Ted Owen, pop and rock expert for Bonhams auction house which put together the collection.
Owen said the Beatles had consistently outsold over the years memorabilia from their only challenger as long-time pop idol, Elvis Presley.
He said the items likely to fetch the highest prices were the Steinway piano, the autographed guitar and a restored Mercedes Benz car owned by Lennon.
He estimated each item would fetch up to $1 million, breaking world records for a single item owned by a rock star and for an instrument used by a pop star.
The memorabilia came from relatives of the Beatles, people who worked with them and collectors eager to cash in on the new wave of Beatle popularity from their "Anthology" series.
